This adds an `onChangeOutputsCreated` callback option (which could replace your async flag) If the callback is specified, it returns the change outputs so change can be recovered async. 

For v2->v3, the option name wouldn't change, and the consumer adding a callback would use the preferSync pathway. We don't need to add the plumbing for the callback into v2 - just note that it's a flag in v2 and will become a full callback in v3.

Otherwise we end up with two options to achieve the same thing (or a breaking change right after the option is put in).

Crypto library has been reorganized and simplified - and all types de-duplicated from the shared model types (closes #289).

It has a barrel out of the main crypto folder to simplify internal imports... and the module packages are now aligned with the NUTS they represent (the cashu-ts/crypto entrypoint now points to the core functions).

The src/index does NOT export from crypto (as before), so the API Extractor still doesn't "see" the contents (as they are not public API for the main library).

So we need to decide - either keep crypto as an "opt-in" set of packages for advanced consumers (= better tree shaking and shorter build times for casual consumers) or whether to drop the modular packages and export all from the main entry point (would close #322 and allow IIFE consumers access to crypto functions).

I don't think crypto module is particularly "heavy", so can make a case either way. 

**EDIT:** - we agreed to remove the sub-exports and export all from the main entry point.

Essentially, v2 had two separate problems:

1. Our old post-processor was wrongly adding .js extensions inside type declaration files (.d.ts), as you highlighted. Type declarations should always be extensionless so TS can resolve index files.

2. NodeNext resolution combined with our submodule exports map meant some named types were not reliably discoverable from the package root, especially for subpaths. This made NodeNext and API Extractor unhappy.

As I understand it, by design, NodeNext + an exports map hides internal files unless we surface them explicitly. That’s good for encapsulation, but it also means tooling cannot “wander” the tree, it needs a clear entry point.

Essentially, v2 had two separate problems:

1. Our old post-processor was wrongly adding .js extensions inside type declaration files (.d.ts), as you highlighted. Type declarations should always be extensionless so TS can resolve index files.

2. NodeNext resolution combined with our submodule exports map meant some named types were not reliably discoverable from the package root, especially for subpaths. This made NodeNext and API Extractor unhappy.

As I understand it, by design, NodeNext + an exports map hides internal files unless we surface them explicitly. That’s good for encapsulation, but it also means tooling cannot “wander” the tree, it needs a clear entry point.

So the new post-process file:

- Strips .js from all relative specifiers in .d.ts, and only ever adds .js to runtime .js files if needed.
- generates a small, explicit lib/types/index.d.ts that re-exports everything from the rolled types entry, and
- adds a few subpath shim .d.ts files to mirror the package.json exports.

This makes TypeScript and tools like API Extractor consistently “see” the public surface.

The post-process result looks like this:

```
lib/
├─ crypto/
│  ├─ client/
│  │  ├─ index.es.js
│  │  └─ index.cjs
│  ├─ common/
│  │  ├─ index.es.js
│  │  └─ index.cjs
│  ├─ mint/
│  │  ├─ index.es.js
│  │  └─ index.cjs
│  └─ util.es.js
├─ cashu-ts.es.js
├─ cashu-ts.cjs
└─ types/
   ├─ cashu-ts.d.ts                 ← rolled types entry from vite-plugin-dts
   ├─ index.d.ts                    ← ADDED, explicit front door that re-exports
   ├─ crypto/
   │  ├─ client/
   │  │  ├─ index.d.ts              ← ADDED shim, mirrors exports subpath
   │  │  └─ client.d.ts
   │  ├─ common/
   │  │  ├─ index.d.ts              ← ADDED shim, mirrors exports subpath
   │  │  └─ common.d.ts
   │  ├─ mint/
   │  │  ├─ index.d.ts              ← ADDED shim, mirrors exports subpath
   │  │  └─ mint.d.ts
   │  └─ util.d.ts                  ← emitted by dts plugin
   │
   │   util/
   │     ├─ index.d.ts              ← ADDED shim, keeps legacy shape working
   │     └─ utils.d.ts              ← ADDED shim, covers package.json mapping note
   │
   ├─ models/
   │  └─ types.d.ts                 ← CLEANED, extensionless specifiers inside
   └─ ... other .d.ts files ...     ← CLEANED, extensionless specifiers inside

```

It’s not an issue in v3 because we dropped the submodule exports entirely. There’s now a single rolled declaration bundle at lib/types/index.d.ts and no need for shims. With only one public entry point, NodeNext and API Extractor resolve the types without ambiguity, and our post-process just makes sure .d.ts specifiers stay extensionless.

The key problem with this approach is that at the point where you do `.sendOutput.xxx` or `.keepOutput.xxx` you are now in an OutputTypeBuilder, not a SendBuilder. So your code won't chain fluently as per your example. 

```ts
wallet.ops.send()
.sendOutput.asRandom()           // you are now in an OutputTypeBuilder
.keepOutput.asDeterministic()    // so this SendBuilder command doesn't chain
.run();
```
You would then need to compose each outputType separately and have an injector (eg: `as()` / `keepAs()` ), like we do for P2PKBuilder.

```ts
const sendOT = wallet.ops.send().sendOutput.asRandom().toOutputType();
const keepOT = wallet.ops.send().keepOutput.asDeterministic().toOutputType();
wallet.ops.send().as(sendOT).keepAs(keepOT).run();
```

Which is a bit verbose IMO, and means three SendBuilders were instantiated.

That's why I opted to declare all the methods in each builder. The extra 150 lines of code in WalletOps makes for much better DX (and clearer TSDOCS), and probably fewer lines of code overall in the consumer app.

Oh, great point. I missed that. We could fix that by giving `OutputTypeBuilder` a reference to the enclosing builder. Then it could return the reference and still allow chaining.

Send does not have a `proofsWeHave` config... it is a `receive()` / `mint()` concept only.

The logic for adding it for `send()` (at least in my head) is that if you are passing in a bunch of proofs, and the Wallet is doing selection and swap, there is a natural `proofsWeHave` - which is the **unselected proofs**.

I believe the wallet SHOULD optimize the swap change against that set.

Why? Because if the consumer already had the smaller proofs, they would have provided them and saved a swap fee.

Using your example:

Pass in 3 proofs (16, 4, 1) to send 6 sats:

Coin selection: 16
Unselected: 4,1

Swap 16 -> 4,2 to send, and the remaining 10 is "change"

So how to split that change? The consumer can't have any singles, because otherwise they would have sent them... 
So let's optimize their change for them to reach target denominations (3 of each proof).

send: 4,2
keep: unspent 1,4 and 10 split according to  targets 1,1,2,2,2,2

We could add a `SendConfig` bool flag (eg: `optimizeChange:boolean` that allows this feature to be switched on or off. I don't mind which is the default, but false would probably be the happy halfway path by keeping it opt-in

Note for our future selves. We decided to use the `onChangeOutputsCreated` as a flag because:

- v2 consumers could only synchronously await the result. There was no 'fire and forget' option before v3.
- The `onChangeOutputsCreated` callback in combination with the `completeMelt` method allows clients to choose async.
- The `prefer-async` header only makes sense in an async operation (ie MUST be used with `onChangeOutputsCreated`)
- Change outputs **would be lost** if a consumer did `prefer-async` but did not use `onChangeOutputsCreated` for the blanks.

We did consider the case where a client might want to store the blanks, but await the operation synchronously... perhaps as a protection against network failure etc.

However, it is already possible to await the async `meltQuotePaid` event and then run the `meltCompleted` method. 

We therefore decided to "fail safe" and prevent the possiblity of lost change.

Nice work @zk-bits - I'll go though it in more detail later. I see noble requires .js for ESM.

Our `post-process-dts.js` script SHOULD add the extensions for ESM automatically, allowing us to keep extensionless imports in TS. Did you try it without adding them all manually, or do we have a problem with the post processing?

This is documented in Noble's v2 changelog as a breaking change for ESM compatibility.

I tried without the .js extensions and then run `npm run compile`  and got TypeScript errors:

```bash
TS2307: Cannot find module '@noble/curves/secp256k1' or its corresponding type declarations.
TS2307: Cannot find module '@noble/hashes/sha2' or its corresponding type declarations.
```

Noble v2 changed their package exports to require explicit .js extensions. The post-process-dts.js script, if I understand it properly, handles relative internal imports (./file)

AFAIK, the issue only arises where we can't guarantee the bytes are in range `n` and then use them for point operations.

`secp256k1.utils.randomSecretKey()` ensures the bytes are in range `n`

So, where doing point multiplication on bytes representing a secret key, if that secret key wasn't guaranteed generated in a way that is safe - such as `secp256k1.utils.randomSecretKey()`, we absolutely should use `secp256k1.Point.Fn.fromBytes()`.

So I think you are correct for:

- src/crypto/NUT01.ts - verifyProof()
- src/crypto/NUT12.ts - verifyDLEQProof()
- src/crypto/core.ts - createBlindSignature(),
- src/crypto/core.ts - blindMessage()  - for `r` param passed in

These are ok, I believe:

- src/model/OutputData.ts - createSingleDeterministicData()
Should not be crypto aware - the fix should be in the crypto library (blindMessage)
- src/crypto/NUT26.ts - deriveP2BKBlindingFactor() - actually called: `deriveP2BKBlindingTweakFromECDH`
Guards out of range as part of the spec - does not silently mod n

### deriveP2BKBlindingFactor (?)

I think you are looking at an out-of-date codebase, because `deriveP2BKBlindingFactor` was an interim function that was renamed in the finalization of P2BK to `deriveP2BKBlindingTweakFromECDH` - which is in both `main` and `development`.

In `deriveP2BKBlindingTweakFromECDH`, we made a conscious decision NOT to make `r` modulo `n` as it was not possible to easily do the same in CDK (Rust language). Instead, we specifically guard against `r === 0n || r >= secp256k1.Point.CURVE().n`.

So it is safe to use `bytestonumber`, and actually part of spec to ensure invalid `r` isn't silently corrected `mod n` in one implementation and left invalid in another, causing a mismatch. Instead, we just throw if we get two out of range `r`s in a row (which is extraordinarily unlikely).

### blindMessage

This one is tricky. It's only used with r param by `createSingleDeterministicData`, but is part of the API, so we can't be sure that other consumers are using it or not.

NUT-00 doesn't specify the range/handling for `r`. So:

- We could just add a range guard here, as per `deriveP2BKBlindingTweakFromECDH` and throw if suppled `r` is out of range. That's the belt and braces approach... give us garbage, we throw it out.
- Alternatively, we can  juggle the `r` to silently make it mod n . This would mean every deterministic `r` generated from a seed valid, but might be incompatible if other implementations handle differently.

The v2 version (https://github.com/cashubtc/cashu-ts/pull/430) includes a change to [src/crypto/client/NUT11.ts](https://github.com/cashubtc/cashu-ts/pull/430/files/9a7e11af7afd3aa8f6c8f919b3d0d21cfca590db#diff-c5e37c2aeef0e3708a646292e027bde4d3ee33e918c9058f4f6560029b46722f) that widens `signP2PKProof` signature from:

```ts
signP2PKProof(proof: Proof, privateKey: string, message?: string): Proof
```

to

```ts
export const signP2PKProof = (proof: Proof, privateKey: string | Uint8Array): Proof
```

with a normalizer:

```ts
// Convert hex string to Uint8Array, or use Uint8Array directly
```

1. Coordinator constructs transaction and embeds digest/mts in the witness of proof(s) to be signed

Update from the Cashu-TS dev meeting... we discussed whether a better approach might be to find a way to pass around a subset of the `SwapPreview` / `MeltPreview` objects, allowing signing from those rather than using the token format and passing around the proof-to-sign with the MTS/digest in its witness field.

## Core Idea

Use a sanitized subset of SwapPreview / MeltPreview as the transport format for signing.
→ Strip all secret/blinding material
→ Keep only the data needed to reconstruct the exact message to sign (MTS)
→ Serialize (e.g. base64 / optional JSON schema version) for easy sharing

Essentially, the minimal wallet requirement in that scenario would be something like:

- method to extract MTS data from the Preview objects and serialise into a `SigningPackage` for sending around
- method to "rehydrate" this into a form that signP2PKProofs / buildP2PKSigAllMessage can use, sign and repackage
- method to merge the signatures into the original preview for completion of transaction

Example `SigningPackage` object:

```ts
{
  version: "cashu-sigall-v1",
  type: "swap" | "melt",
  quote?: string,                 // melt only
  inputs:  [proof1, proof2, ...], // Proof[]
  outputs: [{ amount, B_ }, ...], // subset of OutputData
  messageDigest?: string,         // hex SHA256
  witness?: {                     // ← added after signing starts
    signatures: string[]          // hex signatures
  }
}
```

> * my question is what exactly should mts contain ? and won't it's data leak transaction data ? should we prioritize using the digest here if its available?

mts contains the concatenation of inputs (proofs) and outputs (amounts + blindedMessages) [as per NUT-11](https://github.com/cashubtc/nuts/blob/main/11.md#message-aggregation-for-sig_all)

> * when mts and digest exist must wallets confirm that SHA256(mts) == digest or is there a default we should pick at this point?

That was [in the original PR](https://github.com/cashubtc/nuts/pull/318). But in new scheme, we would pass around a stripped down preview object with just the MTS materials (see the example `SigningPackage ` above).

> * are we enforcing the convention of embedding the `mts/digest` in the first proof alone to avoid ambiguity? that means if multiple proofs contain `mts/digest`, we reject and throw an error ?

In the new scheme, this would be a design decision. I suspect we might want to collate signatures in the object then inject them into first proof when merging back into the original Preview object, as that avoids complications. (see the example `SigningPackage ` above)

> * i also noticed signP2PKProofs currently signs against three different message formats due to SIG_ALL being in flux any idea how we should handle this for or multi-party coordination ?

We can continue to sign all three - and remove the deprecated ones in v4. A mint doesn't care how many signatures, only that enough are valid for each signer expected.

great point on the `RateLimit` / `RateLimit-Policy` headers, good catch that these can appear on any response, not just 429s. I'm looking at the IETF draft now to understand the full shape of them.

for the global store idea, I think it maps nicely to how `requestLogger` already works: a lightweight object that gets updated silently on every response, with a public getter — something like:

```ts
let _rateLimitState: RateLimitState | undefined;

export function getRateLimitState(): RateLimitState | undefined {
  return _rateLimitState;
}
```

A few questions worth aligning on before going further:
- should we only handle the standard `RateLimit` / `RateLimit-Policy` headers (IETF draft), or do we also need to account for mints/CDNs that use non-standard equivalents?
- should the store be per-mint (keyed by URL) or global across all mints? Per-mint feels safer if a consumer is talking to multiple mints simultaneously.
- should parsing `RateLimit` headers be a separate concern from `RateLimitError` (two independent pieces), or should they share a single `RateLimitInfo` type that both populate?
- is `RateLimit-Policy` worth parsing now, or just `RateLimit` to keep the scope tight?

Maybe a better design is a `RequestOption` callback, something like:

  onResponseMeta?: (meta: ResponseMeta) => void;

  - ResponseMeta would look something like:

```ts
 type ResponseMeta = {

    retryAfterMs?: number;     // as above
    rateLimitPolicy?: string;    // raw RateLimit-Policy header
    headers: Headers;            // raw response headers
  };
```

Mints can then subscribe in `requestWithAuth()` and expose to consumers in a getter.

Thanks for your first contribution @4xvgal - appreciate you spending time on cashu-ts!

However, in this instance, I don’t think this is the right fix. `ensure()` was never intended to guarantee the full requested count across multiple mint rounds; it was designed to top up within the hard limits imposed by the mint’s `bat_max_mint` and the instance `maxPerMint`.

In that model, a request larger than those limits is just a bounded best-effort call, not a bug.

Both `maxPerMint` and `desiredPoolSize` are configurable by the consumer, so it's a consumer-configured constraint if `maxPerMint` is so small that it doesn't allow a fill to `desiredPoolSize`.

Changing it to loop until `desiredPoolSize` is reached alters the hot path substantially, because `getBlindAuthToken()` calls `ensure(1)`  under the auth-manager lock.

That means a single protected request can now trigger multiple sequential `/v1/auth/blind/mint` calls before returning one BAT, which introduces avoidable latency and rate-limit/DoS risk.

I think the right fix here is to clarify the contract/docs for `ensure()` rather than change it into a multi-round refill loop.

If there is any bug, it's that `createAuthWallet` doesn't set the `maxPerMint` along with the `desiredPoolSize`.

That's probably where you are surfacing the discrepancy you are trying to fix.

If it set both to `options?.authPool ?? 10` then the AuthManager would at least have a coherent set of hard limits to work with.

Thanks for opening this as a draft. It's an interesting concept.

As requested, I’m treating this draft as a prototype/reference implementation, not something ready for full maintainer review.

Even if the NUT progresses to acceptance, there are a few high-level blockers before this could become reviewable - flagging now to make it easier for you later.

## Scope

This PR adds a large amount of public Mint/Wallet/KeyChain surface for a very niche application area.

Even with the `wallet.ctf` facade gated behind `enableCtf`, the PR still adds public `Wallet` methods, `Mint` methods, keyset metadata, and keychain behavior that every other consumer would have to carry.

Please keep CTF behind a much narrower experimental boundary, preferably without expanding core `Wallet`/`KeyChain` public surface.

See the `auth` module for the kind of encapsulation I mean.


## Compat overloads in Wallet

The compatibility overloads for the old v3-style methods are also unacceptable. We moved to the generic method-based APIs in v4, and overloading those same names to also behave like the old BOLT11 convenience methods is a step backwards.

It makes the API ambiguous, especially because `AmountLike` includes `string`, and it blurs the distinction between generic payment-method flows and the explicit first-class helpers like `createMintQuoteBolt11()` / `mintProofsBolt11()`.

Please remove the v3 compatibility overloads entirely.

## API

The public API needs looking at - the API Extractor report shows a bunch of forgotten exports and an explosion of changes in the public API.

## Docs & Tests

Finally, would need to add docs and complete test coverage when the API shape is intentional and stable enough to expose.

Potential NUT spec wording for laddered search (per suggested change 1 in the [nuts#342 discussion](https://github.com/cashubtc/nuts/pull/342#issuecomment-4982629858)): one sentence for the invariant, one worked trace, one pseudocode block in the draft's existing style. Every round is exactly one NUT-09 request.

**Invariant**

> A probe window containing any signature proves T is at or beyond its start; an empty window proves T is below its start, provided derivation gaps stay shorter than the window.

**Worked trace** (w = 25, wallet's unknown T = 5000; `##` = signatures returned, `--` = empty):

```
Round 1 - ladder (one request): windows at 0 and w*2^k, doubling across the space
 start:  0   25   50  100  200  400  800 1600 3200 6400 12800 ... 2^31
         ##  ##   ##  ##   ##   ##   ##   ##   ##   --    --       --
                                       last hit^    ^first empty
 => T is in (3224, 6400)

Round 2 - grid (one request): 12 windows spread evenly across the bracket
 start:  3469 3713 3957 4202 4446 4690 4934 5179 5423 5667 5911 6155
         ##   ##   ##   ##   ##   ##   ##   --   --   --   --   --
 => T is in (4958, 5179)

Repeat round 2 until grid width is < batch size (in this case no repeat).

Round 3 - tile (one request): the remaining 220 counters, wall to wall
         4959 ............... 5178
         ############---------
 => T = 5000, and its BlindSignature already carries the encrypted d_gap

Round 4 - fetch [T - d_gap, T] in chunks, filter spent per NUT-07
```

**Pseudocode**

```
Probe window (w, default 25). The number of consecutive counters checked at each probe position.
A window containing any signature proves T lies at or beyond its start; an empty window proves T
lies below it. NOTE: w must exceed the wallet's longest run of never-used counters.

Probe budget (budget, default 12). The maximum number of probe windows sent in one search
request. It sets the narrowing rate: each grid round splits the unknown zone into budget + 1
segments, so the search needs one request per ~13x of zone width at the default.

MAX = top of counter space (2^31 for legacy v0 keysets, else 2^32)

 function find_t(keyset_id) {
      // one request: a w-wide window at 0 and at each doubling position
      hits = restore([window(0)] + [window(w * 2^k) for k = 0 .. log2(MAX/w)])
      if (hits is empty) return undefined                  // caller falls back to linear scan
      floor   = highest counter with a signature           // T >= floor
      ceiling = lowest rung start above floor, else MAX+1  // T <  ceiling
      while (floor + 1 < ceiling) {
          zone = (floor + 1, ceiling)                      // width = ceiling - floor - 1
          if (width <= budget * w) {                       // default: width < 300 (12 * 25)
              hits = restore(tile(zone))                   // wall to wall
              floor = highest counter with a signature
              break                                        // zone fully probed: floor is T
          }
          hits = restore(spread(budget, zone))             // 12 probes, ~13x narrowing
          update floor and ceiling from hits
      }
      return floor    // = T; its BlindSignature carries d_gap
  }

```

The trace is generated from the implementation in this PR, not illustrative: rungs at w*2^k, a 12-window grid over the 3176-wide bracket (step 244), and a 220-counter tile.

**Worked example: T = 30,000,000** (defaults: `probeWindow` 25, `probeBudget` 12, `ladderSkip` 0)

*Round 1 (ladder, 1 request).* Windows at 0, 25, 50, 100, ... (25 * 2^k). The rung at 25 * 2^20 = 26,214,400 returns signatures; the next, at 52,428,800, comes back empty.
That brackets T inside a zone ~26.2M counters wide.

*Rounds 2-6 (grid, 1 request each).* Twelve probes spread evenly across the zone divide it into 13 segments, so each round shrinks it by ~13x:

  | Round | Zone width in | Zone width out |
  | ----- | ------------- | -------------- |
  | 2     | 26,214,375    | ~2,016,500     |
  | 3     | ~2,016,500    | ~155,100       |
  | 4     | ~155,100      | ~11,930        |
  | 5     | ~11,930       | ~918           |
  | 6     | ~918          | ~71            |

*Round 7 (tile, 1 request).* The zone is now below the tile threshold (`probeBudget * probeWindow` = 300), so one request probes every counter in it (3 windows, ~71 messages). The highest signature is T exactly, and that reply already carries the encrypted `d_gap`.

*Round 8 (restore, 1 request).* Decrypt `d_gap` (100 in the benchmark) and fetch `[T - 100, T]` as a single 300-counter chunk.

Total: 8 requests for a wallet thirty million counters old, plus the usual NUT-07 state check (= 9 total for 100 `d_gap`). In general the grid needs one round per ~13x of zone width, so even at the u32 ceiling (~4.3e9) it takes 7 grid rounds and ~10 requests overall.

Conflict resolved and force-pushed; `npm run prtasks` green on the v4 lockfile.

Both conflicts came from `MAX_INT_TOKEN_LENGTH`, which sits directly above `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` on main and so got pulled in as context. v4 has never had that cap and should not gain it here: per #887 it changes the default behaviour of a public utility, which is breaking on the LTS line, and v4 has no `decodePayload` so its only exposure is parsing a semi-trusted mint response.

This backport therefore takes only the depth cap: `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH`, the threading through `parseValue`/`parseObject`/`parseArray`, and the two nesting-depth tests. The `rejects oversized integer tokens` test was dropped with the constant (it would fail on v4).

Conflict resolved and force-pushed; `npm run prtasks` green on the v4 lockfile.

All three conflicts were main-only code arriving as diff context. v4 has no `isPaymentRequestSatisfied`, so the settlement guard and its test suite are not carried over: adding that method here would be a v5 feature rather than a fix. An unrelated pre-existing offline-selection test came along with the send-test hunk and was left out too, to keep this to one concern.

What v4 gets is the fix and the speedup:
- `KeyChain.isUnitKeyset(id)`, an O(1) map lookup replacing the per-proof `includes()` scan on the receive path.
- The same check in `selectProofsRGLI` and `selectProofsRotating`, so a proof from another unit of the mint cannot be selected against a target in the wallet's unit.
- `prepareSwapToReceive` keeps its existing behaviour, now via the shared helper.

The direct map lookup is safe here because v4 already has the `Object.create(null)` keyset map from #901; without that a prototype-chain id could slip through.

Conflict resolved and force-pushed; `npm run prtasks` green on the v4 lockfile. Squashed the bot's conflict commit into a single clean one.

The conflict was structural, not context-drag: v4 splits the HMAC path into `deriveHmacSecretAndBlindingFactor` (which calls `deriveHmac` twice, once for the secret and once for the blinding factor), where main derives both in one function. The guard goes at the entry point rather than inside `deriveHmac`, so it runs once per derivation instead of once per HMAC, matching main's placement. `deriveHmac` is private and reached only from there, so nothing bypasses it — including the deprecated `deriveSecret` / `deriveBlindingFactor` exports, which route through the same entry.

Everything else applied cleanly: the `Bytes.writeBigUint64BE` removal, the switch to `numberToBytesBE`, and all three test files. v4 was already importing `numberToBytesBE` in this file and is on the same `@noble/curves` major, so the encoder swap needed no other change.

One deliberate difference from main: the comment on the encoder line says "the caller's guard" rather than "the guard above", because here the guard genuinely lives in the calling function.
